en: Clever at understanding situations and turning them to one's advantage
hook: ASTUTE: A STUDENT who sees through everything.
story: Astute. When Mahin's uncle heard that a new private university would open beside his village market, he did not simply celebrate like everyone else. He quietly rented the empty shop opposite the main gate and turned it into a photocopy and stationery store. Within a year it was the busiest shop in the area. He was astute: clever at understanding situations and turning them to his advantage. Astute observers notice what others miss. Synonyms: shrewd, perceptive, canny.

gre.s: The investor proved remarkably ____: while others panicked and sold, she quietly bought shares she knew were undervalued and tripled her money within a year.
gre.clue: while others panicked and sold

example: An astute coach, Rahima noticed that the opposing bowler tired after five overs and told her batters to wait him out.

en: Bold and shameless, without any embarrassment
hook: BRAZEN: hard and shiny like BRASS, shameless.
story: Brazen. During the final exam, a student copied answers from his neighbour's sheet. Not quietly, not secretly, but openly, turning his whole head while the invigilator stood three metres away. When she stared at him, he smiled and waved. The hall gasped. That was brazen: bold and completely shameless, with no embarrassment at all. Brazen comes from brass, hard and shiny. A brazen lie is told straight to your face.

gre.s: Rather than hiding the forgery, the art dealer made a ____ attempt to sell it at the very gallery that owned the original.
gre.clue: Rather than hiding the forgery

example: In a brazen lie, the company called its river clean on the same day reporters filmed dead fish beside its outlet pipe.

en: Abundant; existing in large amounts
hook: COPIOUS: so many COPIES that there's plenty for all.
story: Copious. Ishita took copious notes in every lecture: three colour-coded pens, diagrams in the margins, and summaries at the end of each page. By the end of the semester she had filled five thick notebooks. When exams arrived, the whole class lined up outside her room asking for photocopies. Copious means plentiful, existing in large quantities. Copious tears, copious rain, copious food at a Bangladeshi wedding. Think: so many copies that there is plenty for everyone.

gre.s: Far from being sparse, the explorer's journals are ____, documenting every plant, river, and conversation she encountered.
gre.clue: Far from being sparse

example: Copious rain in July filled the reservoirs around Rangamati, ending weeks of fear about a water shortage.

en: Warm, friendly, and polite
hook: CORDIAL: from the HEART (cor, as in cardiac).
story: Cordial. Everyone expected the two rival company owners to glare at each other at the business conference. Instead, they shook hands warmly, asked about each other's families, and shared a table at lunch, laughing about old times. They competed fiercely in the market but respected each other personally. Their relationship was cordial: warm, friendly, and polite. Cor means heart, as in cardiac. A cordial invitation comes sincerely from the heart.

gre.s: Though the negotiations were tense, relations between the two delegations remained ____, and each side thanked the other warmly at the close.
gre.clue: each side thanked the other warmly

example: Although the two former partners rarely agreed on business, their emails stayed cordial, always ending with good wishes for each other's families.

en: Pretending to be shy; reluctant to give details
hook: COY: playing it COOL and shy.
story: Coy. When Nadia's friends asked whether she was engaged, she smiled, looked at the floor, and said, 'Maybe, maybe not,' while her cheeks turned pink. She clearly wanted them to keep guessing. She was being coy: pretending to be shy, or reluctant to give details. A company can also be coy about its profits, refusing to give exact numbers. Coy comes from the same Latin root as quiet. Synonyms: evasive, reticent, demure.

gre.s: The minister was uncharacteristically ____ about her plans, deflecting every question about the coming election with a smile and a vague remark about the weather.
gre.clue: deflecting every question

example: The author was coy about the ending of her next novel, saying only that readers should keep some tissues nearby.

en: To distribute; to provide (a service)
hook: DISPENSE: like a water DISPENSER giving out water.
story: Dispense. At the clinic on a remote char island, the only nurse, Shefali Apa, sits behind a wooden table every morning. She checks blood pressure, cleans wounds, and dispenses medicines from a metal cabinet to a long line of patients. To dispense is to distribute or provide. Pharmacists dispense prescriptions, machines dispense tickets, and judges dispense justice. Watch for dispense with, which means to do without: let us dispense with formalities. Synonyms: distribute, allocate, administer. Opposite: withhold.

gre.s: Rather than stockpile the scarce grain, the village council chose to ____ it equally among all households, giving each family the same small ration.
gre.clue: giving each family the same small ration

example: Machines on every platform of the new metro dispense single-journey cards in less than ten seconds.

en: A person who opposes official policy, especially of an authoritarian state
hook: DIS-SIDE-ent: on the other SIDE.
story: Dissident. Under a military regime, a young journalist kept publishing articles that criticised the generals, even after her newspaper was shut down. She printed leaflets at night, was arrested twice, and finally had to flee the country. Yet her essays kept circulating. She was a dissident: a person who openly opposes official policy, especially in an authoritarian state. Dissident comes from dissent, to disagree. As an adjective, we speak of dissident voices or dissident writers. Opposite: loyalist.

gre.s: The regime claimed to tolerate free speech, yet any ____ who criticized its policies in print could expect to be imprisoned or forced into exile.
gre.clue: who criticized its policies in print

example: After years in exile, the dissident novelist returned home to find her books finally sold openly in the capital's shops.

en: Outstandingly bad; shocking
hook: EGREGIOUS: so bad it stands out from the herd (e-greg = out of the flock).
story: Egregious. In the final minute of the match, the striker tumbled to the ground in the penalty box. The referee pointed to the spot. Penalty. But the replay showed clearly that no defender had touched him; he had simply thrown himself down. Millions of viewers screamed at their TVs. The error was egregious: shockingly, glaringly bad. Egregious comes from the Latin for standing out from the flock. An egregious mistake is not small; it is outrageous.

gre.s: The auditors uncovered an ____ error in the accounts, a miscalculation so large that it had inflated profits by millions.
gre.clue: so large that it had inflated profits by millions

example: Attributing a famous quotation to the wrong president was an egregious slip for a history professor writing in a national newspaper.

en: Puzzling and mysterious; hard to explain or read
hook: ENIGMA = a riddle. ENIGMATIC = like a riddle.
story: Enigmatic. Visitors stand in front of the Mona Lisa for minutes, trying to read her face. Is she smiling? Sad? Teasing? Bored? Centuries later, people still argue, because the expression refuses to be pinned down. That is enigmatic: mysterious and difficult to understand. An enigma is a riddle. An enigmatic person keeps everyone guessing about what they really think. Your quiet classmate who never explains anything might be enigmatic too.

gre.s: Scholars still debate the meaning of the poem's ____ final line, which seems to contradict everything that came before it.
gre.clue: Scholars still debate the meaning

example: The only clue was an enigmatic chalk symbol on the warehouse door, unlike anything the detectives had seen before.

en: Making one feel very happy, excited, and energized
hook: EXHILARATING: EX-HILARIOUS, full of joy.
story: Exhilarating. Strapped into a paraglider on a hilltop in Bandarban, Zayan's heart pounded. Then he ran, his feet left the ground, and suddenly he was soaring above the green valleys, wind rushing past his ears, clouds below him. He shouted with pure joy. Afterward, he could not stop smiling for hours. The flight was exhilarating: making him feel thrilled, happy, and full of energy. Opening a GRE score of 330 is exhilarating too.

gre.s: For the young climbers, reaching the summit was ____, a moment of pure joy after weeks of exhausting effort.
gre.clue: a moment of pure joy

example: Watching Bangladesh chase down a huge total in the final over was exhilarating for the packed crowd at Mirpur.

en: Often changing one's mind, likes, or loyalties
hook: FICKLE: FLICKERS like a candle.
story: Fickle. Last year the whole neighbourhood adored a young cricketer. Posters of him hung in every tea stall. Then he scored zero in two matches, and overnight the same fans tore down his posters and cheered a new hero. Public affection is fickle: changing frequently, especially in loyalty or affection. Dhaka's weather in April is fickle too, sunny one hour and stormy the next. Contrast with steadfast, which means firmly loyal. Synonyms: capricious, inconstant.

gre.s: Politicians who rely on the ____ support of voters soon learn that a single unpopular decision can turn yesterday's admirers into tomorrow's opponents.
gre.clue: turn yesterday's admirers into tomorrow's opponents

example: Mountain weather is fickle, so the guide packed rain jackets even though the morning sky was perfectly clear.

en: Not literal; using figures of speech like metaphors
hook: FIGURATIVE: a FIGURE of speech.
story: Figurative. When Shuvo's mother said he had a mountain of homework, his little sister ran to the window looking for the mountain. She took the phrase literally. But their mother was speaking in a figurative way: not literal, using a figure of speech. Metaphors, similes and exaggerations are all figurative language. Telling an actor to break a leg is figurative; nobody wants an actual broken leg. The opposite of figurative is literal. Synonyms: metaphorical, symbolic.

gre.s: Readers who interpret the poet's 'burning city' as an actual fire miss the point; the phrase is ____, describing the speaker's rage rather than any real blaze.
gre.clue: describing the speaker's rage rather than any real blaze

example: Learners of English often stumble over figurative expressions such as 'break the ice', reading them word by word.

en: New and inexperienced; a young bird just learning to fly
hook: FLEDGLING: a baby bird just getting its feathers.
story: Fledgling. Each spring, a pair of mynas nests under the roof of Rupa's house. One morning she saw a fledgling on the windowsill: a young bird, newly feathered, flapping its wings but too scared to leap. Three days later, it flew to the guava tree. As an adjective, fledgling means new and inexperienced: a fledgling business, a fledgling democracy. A fledgling has only just fledged, or grown its flying feathers. Synonyms: budding, novice, nascent. Opposite: veteran.

gre.s: Like many ____ enterprises, the start-up struggled during its first year, lacking both the experience and the capital that established competitors enjoyed.
gre.clue: lacking both the experience and the capital that established competitors enjoyed

example: The fledgling theatre company in Rajshahi staged its first play in a school hall, with borrowed costumes and folding chairs.

en: Filled with something undesirable; causing anxiety
hook: FRAUGHT: FREIGHT-loaded with danger.
story: Fraught. The night before the final match, the dressing room was fraught with tension. Two players had quarrelled, the captain was injured, and the coach's job depended on the result. Nobody slept. Fraught means filled with something undesirable, such as danger, tension or difficulty, and it is often followed by with. Used alone, it means causing anxiety, as in a fraught conversation. It shares a root with freight: heavily loaded. Synonyms: laden, tense, charged.

gre.s: The negotiations were ____ with danger from the start: a single careless word from either side could have reignited a war that had only just ended.
gre.clue: a single careless word from either side could have reignited a war

example: Moving their parents to Dhaka was a decision fraught with guilt for the siblings, who had once promised never to leave the village.

en: Quick to believe things, and so easily fooled
hook: GULLIBLE: like a sea GULL that swallows anything thrown at it.
story: Gullible. A text message arrived on Kamal's uncle's phone: 'Congratulations! You have won fifty lakh taka in a lottery. Send two thousand taka to claim your prize.' He had never bought a lottery ticket, yet he sent the money at once. Of course, there was no prize. He was gullible: easily deceived or tricked. Picture a hungry gull, a seabird that swallows anything thrown to it. Scammers hunt for gullible victims. Synonyms: credulous, naive.

gre.s: Far from being ____, the investigator questioned every claim the witness made, insisting on documents for even the most trivial details.
gre.clue: questioned every claim the witness made

example: Fake websites selling cheap concert tickets target gullible teenagers, who often discover the fraud only at the stadium gate.

en: To stir people up to violence or law-breaking
hook: INCITE: light a fire INSIDE the crowd.
story: Incite. A fake video spread online claiming that a factory had poisoned the local river. Within hours, a man with a megaphone was shouting outside the factory gates, urging the crowd to break in and burn the warehouse. Police later charged him with inciting violence: stirring up and encouraging unlawful behaviour. Incite and excite share a root meaning to set in motion, but you incite people to do something, usually something bad. Synonyms: provoke, instigate, foment.

gre.s: Prosecutors argued that the pamphlets were written not merely to criticize the government but to ____ riots, pointing to passages that urged readers to burn public buildings.
gre.clue: urged readers to burn public buildings

example: The club banned a group of supporters for using social media to incite fights with rival fans after matches.

en: To put someone or something in danger
hook: JEOPARDIZE: put it in JEOPARDY.
story: Jeopardize. Two months before his final exams, Arif started playing online games until four every morning. His grades fell, he missed classes, and the scholarship committee sent him a warning letter. His habit was jeopardizing his scholarship: putting it in danger. Jeopardy means danger. It comes from an old French phrase for an evenly divided game, which you could just as easily lose as win. Something in jeopardy is at risk. Synonyms: endanger, imperil, threaten.

gre.s: Officials warned that any further delay would ____ the entire bridge project, since the foreign loan would be withdrawn if construction had not begun by March.
gre.clue: since the foreign loan would be withdrawn

example: Leaking the exam questions could jeopardize the careers of every teacher at the school, even those who knew nothing about it.

en: To hate something or someone very strongly
hook: LOATHE: 'LOW-THE' — so low in your opinion that you hate it.
story: Loathe. Lamia loathes bitter gourd. One bite and her whole face twists as if she has swallowed poison. She would rather skip dinner entirely than eat it, and once hid a whole plate of it inside a flowerpot. To loathe is to hate something intensely, with disgust. Careful: loathe, ending in e, is the verb, to hate. Loath, without the e, is an adjective meaning reluctant. She was loath to eat it because she loathes it.

gre.s: Though he came to ____ the city's noise and crowds, the poet found he could not write anywhere else.
gre.clue: Though he came to

example: Most cats loathe water, which is why bathing them usually ends with scratched arms and a soaked bathroom floor.

en: To intervene to help resolve a dispute
hook: MEDIATE: stand in the MIDDLE.
story: Mediate. Two families in a village near Bogura had argued for years over the boundary between their fields. Fights broke out at every harvest. Finally the old schoolteacher, respected by both sides, agreed to mediate. He listened to each family, walked the land with them, and proposed a fair line that both accepted. To mediate is to intervene between parties to help resolve a dispute. A mediator stands in the middle, from the Latin medius. Synonyms: arbitrate, intercede, broker.

gre.s: Because neither side trusted the other enough to negotiate directly, both agreed to let a neutral diplomat ____ the dispute over the contested border.
gre.clue: neither side trusted the other enough to negotiate directly

example: A retired judge was asked to mediate between the garment workers' union and the factory owners after wage talks collapsed.

en: Not literal; using one thing to represent another
hook: METAPHORICAL: uses a METAPHOR.
story: Metaphorical. Before the final, the coach looked at his players and said, "This team has the heart of a lion." A new player looked confused. Did someone actually have a lion's heart? The captain laughed and explained. Coach did not mean it literally. He was being metaphorical: using one thing to represent another, here, a lion's heart for courage. Metaphorical means figurative, not literal. Poetry is full of metaphorical language.

gre.s: When the poet describes the city as a cage, she is speaking in ____ terms, not complaining about any actual bars.
gre.clue: not complaining about any actual bars

example: The shattered mirror in the film's last scene is metaphorical, standing for the family that has broken apart.

en: To cancel out the effect of something, making it harmless
hook: NEUTRALIZE: make NEUTRAL, neither acid nor base.
story: Neutralize. During a chemistry practical, Shuvo spilled a few drops of acid on the bench. The lab assistant calmly sprinkled baking soda over it. The fizzing stopped, and the acid became harmless. The baking soda had neutralized it: made it ineffective with an opposite force. Outside the lab, the word works too: a goalkeeper neutralizes a striker, and a calm reply neutralizes an attack. Think neutral: neither side wins. Synonyms: counteract, offset, nullify.

gre.s: Her rivals hoped the scandal would sink the senator's campaign, but her swift and candid apology served to ____ its effects almost entirely.
gre.clue: swift and candid apology

example: Farmers add lime to their fields to neutralize soil that has grown too acidic after years of heavy fertiliser use.

en: To repeat something already said, usually to stress it
hook: RE-ITERATE: say it again and again (iterate).
story: Reiterate. At the start of every class, Shuvo's maths teacher wrote the same sentence on the board: 'Read the question twice.' Students rolled their eyes, but every week she reiterated it, because every week someone lost marks by misreading. To reiterate is to say something again, often for emphasis. Iterate already means to repeat, so reiterate means repeating once more. Politicians reiterate their positions, and teachers reiterate rules. Synonyms: repeat, restate, emphasize.

gre.s: Because so many students had ignored the first notice, the principal felt obliged to ____ the warning in a second, more strongly worded letter.
gre.clue: Because so many students had ignored the first notice

example: At the press conference, the captain reiterated that he would retire after the World Cup, ending weeks of rumours.

en: To voluntarily give up or let go
hook: RELINQUISH: RELease and finISH.
story: Relinquish. For fifty years, Mr. Haque ran the textile company he had founded with a single sewing machine. At seventy-five, he finally relinquished control to his daughter, signing the papers with a trembling hand. It was the hardest thing he had ever done. To relinquish is to voluntarily give up or let go of something: power, a claim, a position, or your grip on a rope. Think: release and finish.

gre.s: The aging dictator refused to ____ power, even after losing an election by an overwhelming margin.
gre.clue: even after losing an election by an overwhelming margin

example: The champion boxer chose to relinquish his title rather than fight an opponent he believed had been doping.

en: Firmly decided and refusing to be turned aside
hook: RESOLUTE: full of RESOLVE.
story: Resolute. Tahmina's family wanted her to marry at seventeen. She refused, calmly but firmly, again and again, for two years. She studied through the arguments, took tuition jobs to pay her own fees, and won a place at university. Nothing could change her mind. She was resolute: firmly determined, unwavering. Resolute comes from resolve, a firm decision. A resolute leader does not bend under pressure. Synonyms: determined, steadfast, unwavering, unyielding. Opposites: irresolute, vacillating.

gre.s: Despite years of threats and imprisonment, the activist remained ____ in her demands for reform, refusing every offer of compromise from the government.
gre.clue: refusing every offer of compromise from the government

example: Resolute in her plan to swim the English Channel, Shabnam trained every dawn in the choppy sea off Cox's Bazar.

en: To strike back in response to an attack or insult
hook: RETALIATE: return the TALLY, an eye for an eye.
story: Retaliate. In a friendly match on the hostel lawn, a bowler deliberately hit Tanvir on the shoulder with a bouncer and then laughed. Tanvir's friends urged him to retaliate by bowling bouncers back at the other team. Instead, he scored fifty runs and let his bat answer. To retaliate is to strike back in response to an attack or insult. It comes from the Latin talis, meaning such: like for like, an eye for an eye. Synonyms: avenge, reciprocate, hit back.

gre.s: Fearing that the rival nation would ____ with punishing tariffs of its own, the government hesitated to impose new taxes on imported goods.
gre.clue: with punishing tariffs of its own

example: When the neighbour's goat ate her spinach for the third time, Nanu retaliated by planting chillies all along the fence.

en: Hardly enough; only a small amount
hook: SCANT: SCANTY, hardly enough.
story: Scant. Tanvir bought a flat-pack bookshelf and threw the instruction booklet aside after one glance. Two hours later, the shelf leaned sideways, a drawer would not close, and three screws lay mysteriously on the floor. He had paid scant attention to the instructions: barely any at all. Scant means barely sufficient, very little. There is scant evidence for many viral health claims. Scant rainfall warns farmers that a drought may be coming.

gre.s: The theory has attracted wide popular attention despite ____ evidence, resting on a single study that has never been replicated.
gre.clue: resting on a single study that has never been replicated

example: The rescue team had scant information about the missing hikers, knowing only which valley they had entered.

en: Strong contempt; to reject with contempt
hook: SCORN: SCORE zero on respect.
story: Scorn. When Mahin announced that he would leave his engineering degree to become a potter, his relatives laughed at the dinner table. "Making clay pots? After all that education?" they said with scorn. Five years later, his ceramics sell in galleries in Dhaka and Singapore. Scorn is strong contempt. As a verb, to scorn is to reject or treat with contempt: to scorn advice, to scorn an offer. Synonyms: disdain, derision, contempt. Opposite: admiration.

gre.s: Purists tend to ____ any adaptation of a classic novel, dismissing even the most faithful film versions as cheap imitations.
gre.clue: dismissing even the most faithful film versions as cheap imitations

example: The veteran critic poured scorn on the sequel, calling it a lazy copy stitched together from leftover scenes.

en: Showing sharp judgment, especially in practical matters
hook: SHREWD: sharp as a SHREW's teeth.
story: Shrewd. Anika's mother runs a small sari shop in Mirpur. When a big chain store opened nearby, she did not panic. She noticed that it closed at eight, so she began staying open until eleven, catching office workers on their way home. Her sales doubled. She is shrewd: showing sharp judgment, especially in practical matters like business. Shrewd once meant wicked; today it means clever and canny. Synonyms: astute, canny, sharp.

gre.s: A ____ investor, she sold her shares months before the crash, having recognized warning signs that most analysts had dismissed as insignificant.
gre.clue: having recognized warning signs that most analysts had dismissed

example: A shrewd judge of character, the old headmaster could tell within a minute whether a new teacher would last the year.

en: To go beyond the limits of
hook: TRANS-CEND: climb (scend) ACROSS (trans) the limits.
story: Transcend. Lalon, the mystic singer of Kushtia, lived in a society divided by religion and caste. Yet his songs are sung by Hindus and Muslims, farmers and professors, rich and poor alike. His music transcends those divisions: it goes beyond their limits. Trans means beyond, and the rest comes from a Latin verb meaning to climb, as in ascend. To transcend is to climb beyond. Great art can transcend language and time. Synonyms: surpass, exceed, rise above.

gre.s: The finest translations ____ the limits of a word-for-word rendering; rather than merely copying sentences, they recreate the spirit of the original.
gre.clue: rather than merely copying sentences

example: Great children's books transcend their intended age group, delighting grandparents as much as the grandchildren they read to.

en: Quietly simple and tasteful rather than showy
hook: UNDER-STATED: stated less loudly than it could be.
story: Understated. At the wedding, guests glittered in heavy gold, sequins, and bright silk. Nadia wore a simple white sari with a thin silver border, small pearl earrings, and no other jewellery. Yet she received more compliments than anyone in the hall. Her elegance was understated: presented in a subtle, restrained, effective way. Understated is the opposite of ostentatious. Sometimes less really is more.

gre.s: Unlike the flashy designs of her rivals, the architect's ____ buildings blend quietly into their surroundings.
gre.clue: blend quietly into their surroundings

example: The actor's understated performance, built almost entirely from glances and silences, moved audiences more than any tearful speech.
